title: Keep documents eligible for back-forward restoration
statement: Pages do not register an unload handler, and the code they do register for lifecycle events uses the events that permit restoration, so a back or forward navigation can restore the document instead of refetching it.
rationale: Restoration is the difference between a back navigation appearing instantaneous and repeating the entire load, and a single legacy handler anywhere on the page removes that possibility for the whole document.
implementation: Replace unload handlers with the visibility and page-hide events, and audit third-party bundles for the same pattern since they are the common source. Use browser developer tooling to list the blockers it reports rather than guessing.

verification.method: Navigate away and back in a browser and record whether the tooling reports the document restored or refetched, together with any blocking reason given.

caution: No search surface observes restoration eligibility. It reaches search only indirectly, because restored navigations are included in the field measurements that page experience uses, so the effect claimed here is on the reader and on those measurements.

title: Restore page state from the persisted event
statement: Code that must run when a document is shown again inspects the persisted flag on the show event and takes the restoration path, rather than assuming the load handler will run.
rationale: On a restored document the load sequence does not repeat, so anything the page needed to do on becoming visible - refresh a timer, resume playback, re-read a value - never happens unless the restoration path exists.
implementation: Add the show handler alongside the existing initialisation and branch on the persisted flag, keeping the two paths in one place so they cannot drift. Do not disable restoration in order to make the load path run again.

verification.method: Trigger a restored navigation and confirm the state the page depends on is correct afterwards without a refetch.

caution: This record concerns correctness after restoration rather than any search behaviour, and it is included because the previous record makes restoration possible.

title: Avoid no-store on documents that should be restorable
statement: The no-store directive is applied to documents whose contents must not be retained, and is not applied to ordinary public documents as a general caching habit.
rationale: That directive prevents restoration entirely, so using it where a weaker directive would have served the same purpose gives up instant history navigation for no benefit.
implementation: Review where the directive is set and replace it with the private directive plus revalidation on documents that only needed to avoid shared storage. Keep it on responses containing data that genuinely must not persist on the device.

verification.method: Record the cache directives per document class and correlate them with the restoration outcome the browser reports for the same routes.

caution: Where a page holds data that must not remain on a shared device after logout, keeping the directive is correct and this record does not ask for it to be removed.

title: Revalidate sensitive data after a restored navigation
statement: A restored document that displays session-dependent information confirms the session is still valid and the values still current before presenting them as live.
rationale: A restored document can be arbitrarily old, so a balance, an order state, or a signed-in identity shown from it may describe a session that has since ended.
implementation: On the restoration path, re-fetch the session-dependent values before showing them, and clear or mask them while the check is in flight. Do not resolve this by making the whole document unrestorable if only part of it is sensitive.

verification.method: End a session in one context, restore a previously loaded document in another, and observe whether stale session-dependent values are displayed as current.

caution: This is a correctness and privacy control for restored documents rather than a discoverability control, and no search effect is claimed for it.
